cells.tense: You know what carrying something is worth, and you know when to set it down.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been holding open, set it down in front of someone who should have it, and say you're done with it.
cells.core: Taking something on and setting it down are the same skill, and right now you're doing both. You choose what to pick up — not everything, and not just because it landed on you — and you can feel where almost done turns into done. That's why things move around you without noise. What you run is fed by what you release, so releasing isn't the pause between jobs. It's part of the job. The cost of keeping it is that no one around you learns where the line is unless they watch you stop — and you stop cleanly, so all they see is the clean stop. It looks easy from outside.
cells.sheetLine: You take things on deliberately, and you know how to finish them.
cells.verb: completing a thing by carrying it and knowing when to set it down
cells.place: at the wheel, choosing the direction and answering for it

cells.tense: You're bracing for the moment the next thing lands on you before the current one is even finished.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing you're still guarding, hand it off with the notes you'd give yourself, and don't check it for a full day.
cells.core: You're carrying more than the present moment is asking you to carry, and the extra is all in the future — what might be needed, what might go wrong, what you'd better already be holding. It looks like strength from outside. From inside it's rehearsal. The strong finish you're known for is coming from a version of you who hasn't arrived and keeps having to be here anyway. The cost is that nothing ever gets to be finished — including the thing in front of you, which keeps getting reopened because finished things feel like things you've lost your grip on. You can test this today without deciding anything about the future.
cells.sheetLine: You're already carrying things that haven't been handed to you yet.

cells.tense: You set the carrying down and you've been standing where you left it ever since.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you used to hold and do one ordinary piece of it today, badly and alone, then stop for the day.
cells.core: The finishing power is intact — that hasn't gone anywhere — but standing back is doing the work now, and from outside it can look like having no direction. It doesn't read as avoidance from inside either. It reads as waiting for a clear signal, a reason strong enough to move again, and the reason keeps not coming. What's actually missing isn't the strength to carry. It's the plain, unglamorous practice of picking something up at all, of being in the room with real material that doesn't care what you meant. That's where the strength comes back from — not by deciding to feel strong, but by handling one small real thing and noticing the ground holds.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped carrying and you've been waiting for a reason to start.

cells.tense: You're already choosing what gets carried, and describing it as if it were chosen for you.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person or on paper, that you put a specific thing down on purpose and the ending was your call.
cells.core: You decide all day — yes and no to things — and people around you read those calls as your character. You just don't bill it that way. When something ends, you speak as though it ended, as though the timing came from outside. Here's what you can check: the last time you let something go and then said you had no choice about the timing — whether that's actually true, or whether the timing was yours and saying so felt like taking credit you weren't sure you'd earned. You don't have to take credit. You only have to stop telling the story as though the schedule decided.
cells.sheetLine: You choose what you carry and what you put down. Start admitting it.
